newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech bank woes reflect reform process - cbank gov.
newsitem.headline: Czech bank woes reflect reform process - cbank gov.

text.p: Recent banking problems are a symptom of the entire Czech economic reform process, not an isolated problem limited to the banking sector, central bank Governor Josef Tosovsky on Tuesday.
Speaking to Parliament, Tosovsky said the recent failure of Kreditni Banka and related problems at Agrobanka must be taken in the bigger context of restructuring the economy.
"An idea appeared here that the problems at Kreditni are a problem of the banking sector. But that is not how it is, it must be seen as the banking sector in the context of economic reform," he said.
"The banking sector and its problems are seen alone, but the problem is in the whole financial system, including investment funds, health insurance companies, etc," he added.

In August, the Czech National Bank (CNB) rescinded the licence of the insolvent Kreditni Banka whose losses were estimated at nearly 12 billion crowns after a complicated series of non-performing loans and debt swaps.

CNB then followed in mid-September with the temporary forced administration of Agrobanka, the 12th bank to come under CNB supervision, saying it had become illiquid partly because of its ties to Kreditni and the secretive investment group Motoinvest.

Since then, the banking crisis has become a political football booted between the central bank, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus -- one of the main architects of the reform process -- and the opposition, with each blaming the other.
In his speech, Tosovsky outlined measures the central bank hoped to undertake to bring about greater transparency and confidence in the sagging Czech capital and financial markets.

The CNB has submitted proposals to parliament to create an umbrella markets watchdog including creating a central supervisory organ that would oversee the work of regulators on the banking, insurance and capital markets, including the activities of investment funds.
